classificationHint: Use this for aggressive old-school British rap whose fast, layered breakbeat sound is harder and more abrasive than conventional UK hip-hop.

label: Hip Hop---Cloud Rap
description: Atmospheric hip-hop with hazy production, soft synths, reverb, and often relaxed or melodic delivery.
classificationHint: Use this when the rap production feels dreamy, floating, and low-pressure.

label: Hip Hop---Conscious
description: Hip-hop focused on social, political, reflective, or intellectual lyrical themes.
classificationHint: Use this when lyrical content is clearly thoughtful or socially aware.

label: Hip Hop---Crunk
description: High-energy Southern hip-hop with chant hooks, aggressive club energy, and heavy drums.
classificationHint: Use this when the track is loud, chant-driven, and built for energetic crowd response.

label: Hip Hop---Cut-up/DJ
description: Hip-hop or DJ music built around turntable edits, cut-up samples, and collage-like performance.
classificationHint: Use this when DJ technique and sample cutting are central.

label: Hip Hop---DJ Battle Tool
description: A functional DJ record containing isolated beats, vocal phrases, tones, scratches, or short samples designed for turntable battles and live manipulation.
classificationHint: Use this when the recording is structured as raw material for scratching, beat juggling, or battle routines rather than as a conventional standalone song.

distinguishFrom.label: Hip Hop---Turntablism
distinguishFrom.difference: Turntablism is the performed musical practice; a DJ Battle Tool is source material specifically prepared for that practice.

distinguishFrom.label: Hip Hop---Cut-up/DJ
distinguishFrom.difference: Cut-up/DJ describes a completed collage-like DJ recording; a Battle Tool supplies isolated elements intended for live manipulation.

label: Hip Hop---Electro
description: Early hip-hop-related electronic music driven by TR-808 rhythms, syncopated machine funk, robotic synths, and often vocoder or talkbox vocals.
classificationHint: Use this when old-school rap or breakdance context combines with crisp 808 programming and a distinctly robotic electro-funk groove.

distinguishFrom.label: Electronic---Electro
distinguishFrom.difference: Both share 808 machine funk; Hip Hop Electro emphasizes rap, breaking, and early hip-hop context, while Electronic Electro can be fully instrumental club music.

distinguishFrom.label: Hip Hop---Miami Bass
distinguishFrom.difference: Miami Bass descends from electro but pushes faster club rhythm and extreme sub-bass; Electro is more robotic and machine-funk centered.

label: Hip Hop---Favela Funk
description: Brazilian baile funk from Rio de Janeiro, centered on Portuguese MC vocals, hard syncopated drum loops, repetitive hooks, and sound-system dance energy.
classificationHint: Use this when Portuguese MC delivery and characteristic baile-funk percussion or tamborzão-derived rhythm are central, rather than simply Latin-influenced rap.

label: Hip Hop---G-Funk
description: West Coast hip-hop style with smooth funk samples, synth leads, relaxed groove, and melodic basslines.
classificationHint: Use this when the production has a laid-back West Coast funk feel.

label: Hip Hop---Gangsta
description: Hip-hop centered on street narratives, hard delivery, and gangsta rap themes.
classificationHint: Use this when lyrical content and delivery clearly fit gangsta rap.

label: Hip Hop---Go-Go
description: Washington, D.C. groove music built around continuous live percussion, syncopated funk rhythm, call-and-response vocals, and audience interaction.
classificationHint: Use this when congas and auxiliary percussion sustain an unbroken live groove with shouted responses or band-leader interaction.

distinguishFrom.label: Funk / Soul---Gogo
distinguishFrom.difference: The sound is the same Washington, D.C. tradition; use the Hip Hop grouping when rap and MC performance dominate, and Funk / Soul when the live band groove dominates.

label: Hip Hop---Grime
description: UK MC style with sparse 140 BPM beats, dark synths, and aggressive delivery.
classificationHint: Use this when rap/MC delivery and grime production are both central.

label: Hip Hop---Hardcore Hip-Hop
description: Aggressive hip-hop with hard beats, forceful delivery, and confrontational energy.
classificationHint: Use this when intensity and aggressive rap style dominate.

label: Hip Hop---Hiplife
description: A Ghanaian fusion of hip-hop with highlife, combining rap—often in Akan or other Ghanaian languages—with highlife melody, rhythm, and local popular-music production.
classificationHint: Use this when Ghanaian-language rap or vocal delivery is integrated with recognizable highlife-derived melodic and rhythmic character.

label: Hip Hop---Horrorcore
description: Hip-hop using horror imagery, dark themes, and disturbing or theatrical lyrical content.
classificationHint: Use this when the track is rap-based and explicitly horror-themed.

label: Hip Hop---Hyphy
description: High-energy Bay Area hip-hop with punchy programmed drums, eccentric synth or bass figures, animated slang-heavy delivery, and a deliberately rowdy party feel.
classificationHint: Use this when Northern California rap identity combines with an exuberant, percussive beat and the restless party energy associated with the hyphy movement.

label: Hip Hop---Instrumental
description: Hip-hop production presented without a lead rap vocal.
classificationHint: Use this when the beat itself is the main track and has clear hip-hop structure.

label: Hip Hop---Jazzy Hip-Hop
description: Hip-hop using jazz samples, jazz harmony, laid-back grooves, or live jazz-influenced instrumentation.
classificationHint: Use this when jazz color is central to the beat or arrangement.

label: Hip Hop---Kwaito
description: South African township dance music that slows house-derived grooves and pairs them with heavy bass, sparse loops, chant-like vocals, and locally rooted rap or spoken delivery.
classificationHint: Use this when a relaxed, bass-heavy house pulse supports South African township vocal style and repetitive call-and-response rather than conventional US hip-hop rhythm.

label: Hip Hop---Miami Bass
description: Fast South Florida hip-hop descended from electro, defined by booming TR-808 low end, brisk programmed rhythms, chant hooks, and club- or dance-oriented rap.
classificationHint: Use this when extremely prominent 808 bass and an uptempo electro-derived groove drive a Miami or bass-music rap track.

label: Hip Hop---Pop Rap
description: Rap music with accessible pop hooks, polished production, and mainstream song structure.
classificationHint: Use this when rap delivery is central but the track is strongly pop-oriented.

label: Hip Hop---Ragga HipHop
description: A fusion of hip-hop production and rap with dancehall or ragga rhythms, Jamaican-style toasting, patois delivery, and reggae-derived vocal phrasing.
classificationHint: Use this when hip-hop beats and rap structure are inseparable from dancehall rhythm or ragga-style toasting; use Dancehall when the reggae framework clearly dominates.

label: Hip Hop---RnB/Swing
description: A crossover of hip-hop beats and contemporary R&B vocals with a pronounced swung rhythmic feel, polished hooks, and late-1980s-to-1990s urban production.
classificationHint: Use this when rap-informed drums and smooth R&B singing share the foreground and the beat has an audible swing rather than a straight contemporary groove.

distinguishFrom.label: Funk / Soul---New Jack Swing
distinguishFrom.difference: The styles substantially overlap; RnB/Swing under Hip Hop foregrounds rap-informed production, while New Jack Swing under Funk / Soul foregrounds the R&B song and vocal tradition.

distinguishFrom.label: Funk / Soul---Swingbeat
distinguishFrom.difference: Swingbeat names the swung R&B production style itself; RnB/Swing is the broader hip-hop-facing crossover category.

label: Hip Hop---Screw
description: The Houston chopped-and-screwed style pioneered by DJ Screw, slowing and lowering recordings while repeating, cutting, or delaying phrases to create a heavy hypnotic flow.
classificationHint: Use this when slowed, pitch-lowered hip-hop also contains deliberate chops, phrase repetition, stop-time, or DJ edits—not for an unedited naturally slow track.

label: Hip Hop---Thug Rap
description: Street-centered rap organized around a hardened outlaw persona, survival, loyalty, violence, and the pressures of criminalized urban life.
classificationHint: Use this when the lyrical identity consistently centers on the 'thug' persona or survival narrative; prefer Gangsta when detailed gang or organized-street narratives are the clearer frame.

label: Hip Hop---Trap
description: Hip-hop style with 808 bass, rapid hi-hats, sparse dark melodies, and modern Southern-influenced production.
classificationHint: Use this when trap drum programming and 808 low-end define the track.

label: Hip Hop---Trip Hop
description: Hip-hop-influenced downtempo style with moody samples, slow beats, and cinematic atmosphere.
classificationHint: Use this when the track is slower and darker than standard hip-hop and closer to trip-hop aesthetics.

label: Hip Hop---Turntablism
description: Hip-hop focused on DJ scratching, beat juggling, and turntable performance as musicianship.
classificationHint: Use this when turntable technique is the primary musical feature.

label: Jazz---Afro-Cuban Jazz
description: Jazz harmony and improvisation organized around Afro-Cuban rhythmic systems such as clave, tumbao, and montuno, typically with congas, bongos, timbales, piano, and horns.
classificationHint: Use this when Cuban clave and percussion actively govern the jazz arrangement rather than appearing as a brief Latin color.

label: Jazz---Afrobeat
description: Extended West African ensemble music combining interlocking percussion, cyclical guitar and bass, horn riffs, improvisation, funk drive, and often politically charged vocals.
classificationHint: Use this when a long, layered groove rooted in West African rhythm and funk supports repeated horn figures and ensemble development rather than conventional jazz swing.

label: Jazz---Avant-garde Jazz
description: Experimental jazz that extends or disrupts conventional harmony, timbre, form, notation, and improvisational practice while retaining a discernible jazz lineage.
classificationHint: Use this broad label when deliberate formal or sonic experimentation is central but the performance is not completely free of composed structure.

label: Jazz---Big Band
description: Jazz for a large arranged ensemble, typically organized into saxophone, trumpet, trombone, and rhythm sections with coordinated riffs, sectional writing, and featured soloists.
classificationHint: Use this when written interplay between large horn sections defines the sound; add Swing only when the rhythmic and historical swing style is also clear.

label: Jazz---Bop
description: Bebop: fast, small-group modern jazz built on intricate melodies, extended chord progressions, asymmetrical accents, and virtuosic improvised solos rather than social dancing.
classificationHint: Use this when rapid harmonic movement, angular heads, interactive rhythm-section accents, and technically dense soloing point to the 1940s bebop language.

label: Jazz---Bossa Nova
description: Brazilian jazz-related style with soft syncopation, gentle guitar rhythm, and smooth vocal or instrumental phrasing.
classificationHint: Use this when the track has clear bossa nova rhythm and light Brazilian jazz feel.

label: Jazz---Cape Jazz
description: South African jazz associated with Cape Town, blending jazz improvisation with local carnival, choir, folk, and dance traditions and often bright, lilting melodic themes.
classificationHint: Use this when South African Cape rhythmic and melodic identity is audible within the jazz arrangement, not merely because the performer is South African.

label: Jazz---Contemporary Jazz
description: A broad category for present-day jazz that uses current composition, production, instrumentation, or cross-genre influence while keeping improvisation and jazz interaction central.
classificationHint: Use this when the performance is clearly modern jazz but no narrower label such as fusion, nu jazz, post-bop, or smooth jazz adequately describes it.

label: Jazz---Cool Jazz
description: A restrained post-bebop style with lighter tone, controlled dynamics, spacious phrasing, intricate arrangements, and a calmer rhythmic surface than hard-driving bop.
classificationHint: Use this when the jazz language is modern but deliberately understated, airy, and compositionally controlled rather than blues-heavy or aggressive.

label: Jazz---Dixieland
description: Traditional New Orleans-style jazz featuring collective front-line improvisation by trumpet, clarinet, and trombone over a two-beat rhythm section and familiar song forms.
classificationHint: Use this when several horns improvise simultaneously in an early-jazz ensemble texture rather than taking isolated modern-jazz solos.

label: Jazz---Easy Listening
description: Polished, unobtrusive orchestral or small-ensemble popular music using smooth melodies, soft dynamics, and jazz-colored harmony without demanding improvisational intensity.
classificationHint: Use this when accessibility and background-listening smoothness are primary; use Smooth Jazz when contemporary jazz soloing and groove remain more prominent.

label: Jazz---Free Improvisation
description: Spontaneously created music without predetermined song form, chord sequence, meter, or necessary stylistic idiom, shaped through real-time listening and interaction.
classificationHint: Use this when the performance is genuinely non-idiomatic and unconstrained; use Free Jazz when recognizable jazz phrasing, instrumentation, or rhythmic language remains central.

label: Jazz---Free Jazz
description: Jazz that loosens or abandons fixed chord changes, regular meter, predetermined form, and conventional solo hierarchy in favor of collective interaction and open improvisation.
classificationHint: Use this when structural freedom is radical but the musicians' phrasing, ensemble practice, and historical language remain recognizably jazz-based.

label: Jazz---Fusion
description: Jazz blended with rock, funk, or electronic elements, often with electric instruments and complex playing.
classificationHint: Use this when jazz improvisation and non-jazz rhythm/production are both central.

label: Jazz---Gypsy Jazz
description: A European swing-guitar tradition associated with Django Reinhardt, featuring acoustic lead guitar, violin or clarinet, walking bass, and percussive rhythm-guitar accompaniment known as la pompe.
classificationHint: Use this when acoustic string instrumentation, la-pompe rhythm, and virtuosic swing phrasing define the ensemble rather than American big-band swing.

label: Jazz---Hard Bop
description: A forceful 1950s extension of bebop that deepens its blues, gospel, soul, and rhythm-and-blues elements through heavier grooves, earthy themes, and assertive small-group improvisation.
classificationHint: Use this when bebop harmony and soloing are present but the groove is more blues-rooted, soulful, and hard-driving than cool jazz or straight bebop.

label: Jazz---Jazz-Funk
description: Jazz improvisation and harmony placed over funk's syncopated bass, strong backbeat, electric keyboards, guitar, horns, and groove-centered repetition.
classificationHint: Use this when funk rhythm is sustained and central but jazz soloing, harmonic language, or ensemble writing remains substantial rather than decorative.

label: Jazz---Jazz-Rock
description: A jazz and rock fusion emphasizing electric guitar, keyboards, amplified rhythm sections, rock backbeats, extended compositions, and substantial jazz improvisation.
classificationHint: Use this when rock instrumentation and rhythmic weight share equal structural importance with jazz harmony and soloing; use Fusion for a broader mix beyond rock.

label: Jazz---Latin Jazz
description: A broad fusion of jazz harmony and improvisation with Latin American and Caribbean rhythmic systems, including Afro-Cuban clave traditions and Brazilian samba or bossa-derived approaches.
classificationHint: Use this when a Latin rhythmic framework governs the jazz performance but the specific Cuban, Brazilian, or other regional branch is uncertain.

label: Jazz---Modal
description: Jazz organized around modes or sustained tonal areas rather than rapid functional chord changes, creating harmonic space for melodic development and extended improvisation.
classificationHint: Use this when solos develop over relatively static modal centers and the reduced rate of chord change is a defining compositional feature.

label: Jazz---Post Bop
description: A 1960s-rooted small-group language combining hard bop with modal, avant-garde, and free-jazz ideas while retaining composed themes, harmonic direction, and interactive swing.
classificationHint: Use this when bop remains the foundation but harmony, form, and ensemble interaction are more open and exploratory without becoming fully free jazz or fusion.

label: Jazz---Ragtime
description: A composed, syncopated piano and ensemble tradition built on march-like left-hand patterns against displaced right-hand accents, historically preceding and influencing early jazz.
classificationHint: Use this when written ragtime syncopation and an alternating march bass dominate; do not require jazz improvisation, which is often minimal or absent.

label: Jazz---Smooth Jazz
description: Polished, relaxed jazz with clean production, soft grooves, and accessible melodic focus.
classificationHint: Use this when the track is gentle, smooth, and radio-friendly rather than improvisationally intense.

label: Jazz---Soul-Jazz
description: Accessible, groove-heavy jazz drawing on gospel, blues, soul, and rhythm and blues, often led by Hammond organ, saxophone, or guitar over repeated riffs and backbeats.
classificationHint: Use this when soulful melody, church-inflected phrasing, and a strong bluesy groove outweigh bop complexity while jazz improvisation remains central.

label: Jazz---Space-Age
description: Mid-century space-age pop and exotica using orchestral jazz colors, unusual percussion, early electronic effects, stereo spectacle, and playful futuristic or lounge imagery.
classificationHint: Use this when retro-futurist studio arrangement and novelty sound design matter more than improvisation; use Easy Listening for smoother music without the space-age concept.

label: Jazz---Swing
description: Dance-oriented jazz characterized by a propulsive swung eighth-note feel, walking bass, riff-based arrangements, and soloists supported by small groups or organized big-band sections.
classificationHint: Use this when the rhythmic swing feel and dance-band language define the performance; Big Band alone describes ensemble size and may use other styles.

label: Latin---Afro-Cuban
description: A broad family of Cuban music in which African-derived rhythmic, percussion, call-and-response, and religious traditions are structurally central to Cuban song or dance forms.
classificationHint: Use this broad label when clave-based Cuban music has especially prominent African-derived percussion or ritual vocabulary but no narrower rumba, son, or Afro-Cuban jazz form is certain.

label: Latin---Axé
description: A high-energy Bahian popular-music style associated with Salvador carnival, combining Afro-Brazilian bloco percussion with dance-pop, samba-reggae, frevo, and Caribbean influences.
classificationHint: Use this for polished carnival-oriented songs driven by dense Bahian percussion, exuberant vocals, and pop hooks; prefer Batucada for percussion-ensemble performances without the axé song format.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Batucada
distinguishFrom.difference: Batucada foregrounds a percussion ensemble; Axé is a vocal carnival-pop song style.

label: Latin---Bachata
description: A Dominican guitar-led song and dance genre with a steady four-beat pulse, syncopated güira and bongó, melodic requinto guitar, and emotionally direct vocals traditionally centered on romance and heartbreak.
classificationHint: Use this when interlocking lead and rhythm guitars, crisp güira, and the characteristic Dominican four-beat dance groove define the track; Bolero is usually slower and less percussion-driven, while Merengue is faster and more propulsive.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Bolero
distinguishFrom.difference: Bolero is slower and smoother; Bachata uses a sharper guitar-led Dominican dance groove.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Merengue
distinguishFrom.difference: Merengue is faster and driven by a continuous duple tambora-güira pulse; Bachata is guitar-led.

label: Latin---Baião
description: A northeastern Brazilian rhythm and song form popularized nationally in the 1940s, typically carried by accordion, zabumba bass drum, triangle, and a distinctive syncopated two-beat groove.
classificationHint: Use this when the compact baião rhythm is identifiable, especially in accordion-led northeastern arrangements; Forró is the broader dance-music family that can also contain xote, xaxado, and other rhythms.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Forró
distinguishFrom.difference: Forró is the broader northeastern dance family; Baião is one specific syncopated rhythm within it.

label: Latin---Batucada
description: A percussion-centered samba practice performed by an ensemble of surdos, caixas, repiniques, tamborims, agogôs, and shakers, producing interlocking carnival rhythms and massed accents.
classificationHint: Use this when the percussion bateria itself is the musical focus, with little harmonic or song material; use Samba for complete songs and Axé for Bahian carnival pop with prominent vocals and hooks.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Samba
distinguishFrom.difference: Samba includes complete song and harmonic forms; Batucada makes the massed percussion bateria the primary content.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Axé
distinguishFrom.difference: Axé is a polished vocal carnival-pop style; Batucada is primarily percussion-ensemble performance.

label: Latin---Beguine
description: A French Caribbean Creole dance-music tradition from Martinique and Guadeloupe, combining local syncopation with nineteenth-century ballroom forms and later performed by clarinet-, string-, or horn-led orchestras.
classificationHint: Use this when French Antillean context and a smooth but syncopated ballroom-derived groove are evident; Compas has a more modern Haitian guitar-band pulse, while biguine-influenced jazz should retain Jazz when improvisation dominates.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Compas
distinguishFrom.difference: Beguine is a French Antillean ballroom-derived tradition; Compas is a modern Haitian guitar-band style.

label: Latin---Bolero
description: A slow, romantic Latin American song and dance form, originating in Cuba and widely adapted across the region, with expressive vocals, measured syncopation, and guitar, trio, orchestral, or tropical accompaniment.
classificationHint: Use this when the sustained romantic vocal and characteristic slow bolero pulse define the performance; Samba-Canção has Brazilian samba phrasing, while Ranchera uses Mexican rural-song delivery and accompaniment.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Samba-Canção
distinguishFrom.difference: Samba-Canção retains Brazilian samba phrasing; Bolero follows the pan-Latin slow bolero pulse.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Ranchera
distinguishFrom.difference: Ranchera uses a distinctly Mexican declamatory song style; Bolero is smoother and broadly pan-Latin romantic song.

label: Latin---Boogaloo
description: A 1960s New York Latin dance style that fused mambo and son-based rhythms with rhythm-and-blues backbeat, soul shouts, bluesy piano and horns, and often bilingual English-Spanish vocals.
classificationHint: Use this when Afro-Cuban percussion and piano riffs meet an unmistakable R&B or soul backbeat and party-vocal format; Mambo lacks the same soul emphasis, while Funk/Soul alone lacks the Latin rhythmic foundation.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Mambo
distinguishFrom.difference: Mambo centers Afro-Cuban big-band dance riffs; Boogaloo adds an explicit R&B backbeat and soul vocal language.

distinguishFrom.label: Funk / Soul---Rhythm & Blues
distinguishFrom.difference: Rhythm & Blues lacks the defining Afro-Cuban percussion, piano montuno, and Latin dance framework of Boogaloo.

label: Latin---Bossanova
description: A late-1950s Brazilian song style that pares samba rhythm into softly syncopated guitar patterns, restrained vocals, subtle percussion, and harmonically sophisticated, jazz-influenced arrangements.
classificationHint: Use this for intimate, understated Brazilian songs with characteristic syncopated guitar and extended harmony; Samba is generally more percussive and extroverted, while MPB is a broader later category.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Samba
distinguishFrom.difference: Samba is generally more percussion-forward and extroverted; Bossanova reduces its rhythm to an intimate guitar pattern.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---MPB
distinguishFrom.difference: MPB is a broad post-1960s Brazilian songwriting field; Bossanova is a specific late-1950s rhythm and aesthetic.

label: Latin---Carimbó
description: An Afro-Indigenous dance and music tradition from Pará in northern Brazil, built around curimbó drums, responsorial singing, hand percussion, and a circular, swaying groove; modern forms may add guitars and horns.
classificationHint: Use this when Pará regional identity and curimbó-led dance rhythm are evident; Lambada developed partly from electrified carimbó but uses a smoother, faster partner-dance arrangement.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Lambada
distinguishFrom.difference: Carimbó is the percussion-rooted Pará tradition; Lambada is its faster, smoother, electrified partner-dance descendant.

label: Latin---Cha-Cha
description: A Cuban social dance style developed from danzón-mambo, marked by a clear medium-tempo pulse, repeated chachachá foot-rhythm in the percussion, and concise melodic charanga arrangements.
classificationHint: Use this when the steady, easily counted cha-cha-cha dance pattern is more prominent than mambo's faster accents or danzón's extended sectional form.

label: Latin---Charanga
description: A Cuban dance-orchestra format centered on flute and violins with piano, bass, timbales, güiro, and vocals, historically associated with danzón, cha-cha-chá, and later charanga-based salsa.
classificationHint: Use this when the light flute-and-violin ensemble color identifies the arrangement; combine it with Danzon or Cha-Cha when the actual dance form is clear.

label: Latin---Choro
description: A Brazilian urban instrumental tradition originating in nineteenth-century Rio de Janeiro, known for agile ornamented melodies, contrapuntal interplay, virtuoso improvisation, and ensembles of flute, guitar, cavaquinho, and pandeiro.
classificationHint: Use this for melody-led Brazilian instrumental performances with rapid ensemble dialogue and improvised variation; Bossanova is quieter and song-centered, while Samba foregrounds vocal or percussion-driven groove.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Bossanova
distinguishFrom.difference: Choro emphasizes virtuoso instrumental melody and ensemble dialogue; Bossanova emphasizes understated song and harmony.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Samba
distinguishFrom.difference: Choro is predominantly melody-led and instrumental; Samba more often foregrounds vocal form or percussion groove.

label: Latin---Compas
description: A modern Haitian dance-band style derived from méringue, built on a steady syncopated pulse, interlocking electric guitars, bass, drums and congas, with horn lines, keyboards, and Haitian Creole vocals.
classificationHint: Use this for the smooth, continuous Haitian guitar-band groove; Beguine belongs to the French Antilles, while Soca is generally more carnival-driven and rhythmically forceful.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Beguine
distinguishFrom.difference: Compas uses a steady modern Haitian guitar-band pulse; Beguine is a French Antillean ballroom-derived style.

distinguishFrom.label: Reggae---Soca
distinguishFrom.difference: Soca is Trinidadian carnival music with a harder rhythmic drive; Compas is smoother Haitian guitar-band dance music.

label: Latin---Conjunto
description: Texas-Mexican conjunto is an accordion-led dance-music tradition built around button accordion, bajo sexto, bass, and drums, performing polkas, waltzes, rancheras, corridos, and related border repertory.
classificationHint: Use this when the small accordion-and-bajo-sexto ensemble and Texas-Mexican dance repertory are central; Norteño is its closely related northern Mexican counterpart, while Tejano often uses a fuller, more commercial band sound.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Norteño
distinguishFrom.difference: Conjunto is the Texas-Mexican branch; Norteño is the closely related northern Mexican tradition.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Tejano
distinguishFrom.difference: Conjunto specifies the small accordion-and-bajo-sexto ensemble; Tejano is a wider Texas-Mexican popular field.

label: Latin---Corrido
description: A Mexican narrative ballad tradition that recounts historical events, conflicts, migrations, notable people, or contemporary street life in direct strophic verses, commonly accompanied by norteño, banda, or mariachi ensembles.
classificationHint: Use this for songs whose sequential storytelling is the defining trait, regardless of accompaniment; use Ranchera for expressive rural-themed song without sustained narrative and Norteño for instrumental style alone.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Ranchera
distinguishFrom.difference: Corrido is defined by sequential narrative; Ranchera is an expressive self-contained song rather than a chronicle.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Norteño
distinguishFrom.difference: Corrido is a narrative song form that can use many ensembles; Norteño identifies the accordion-led regional sound.

label: Latin---Cubano
description: A broad fallback category for Cuban popular and traditional music whose clave-based rhythm, Spanish-language vocal style, and ensemble character are clear but whose precise Cuban form is uncertain.
classificationHint: Use this only when Cuban identity is audible or documented and a narrower Son, Rumba, Mambo, Guaracha, Timba, or other Cuban label cannot be assigned confidently.

label: Latin---Cumbia
description: A Colombian Caribbean dance-music family joining African-derived drums, Indigenous flutes or gaitas, shakers, and a characteristic loping duple pulse, later adapted by orchestras and popular bands throughout Latin America.
classificationHint: Use this when the swaying cumbia pulse is central, whether in traditional flute-and-drum or commercial electric form; Vallenato is accordion-led, and Porro typically has a stronger brass-band identity.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Vallenato
distinguishFrom.difference: Cumbia is rooted in a loping drum-and-flute dance pulse; Vallenato centers accordion, caja, guacharaca, and narrative song.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Porro
distinguishFrom.difference: Porro has a stronger Colombian wind- or brass-band identity; Cumbia is more closely tied to drum-and-gaita foundations.

label: Latin---Danzon
description: A formal Cuban couple-dance descended from contradanza, using an elegant measured tempo and contrasting composed sections, often performed by charanga with later montuno-like finales.
classificationHint: Use this when graceful sectional dance form and charanga orchestration outweigh the repetitive montuno drive of son or the sharper pulse of cha-cha-chá.

label: Latin---Descarga
description: A Cuban improvised jam-session practice in which musicians take extended solos and exchange ideas over repeated son montuno, mambo, rumba, bolero, or Latin-jazz frameworks.
classificationHint: Use this when open-ended improvisation and rotating solo features are the recording's main purpose rather than a tightly arranged dance song.

label: Latin---Forró
description: A broad northeastern Brazilian social-dance family commonly performed by accordion, zabumba, and triangle, encompassing rhythms such as baião, xote, and xaxado and songs about celebration, migration, and regional life.
classificationHint: Use this broad label when the northeastern trio sound and partner-dance function are clear but no single rhythm is dominant; use Baião when its specific syncopated pulse can be identified.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Baião
distinguishFrom.difference: Forró is a broad dance-music family; Baião is one identifiable rhythm inside that family.

label: Latin---Gaita
description: A regional Latin label most often referring either to Colombian Caribbean flute-and-drum music led by the Indigenous gaita duct flute or to Venezuelan gaita zuliana, a choral percussion-rich festive song tradition from Zulia.
classificationHint: Use only when Colombian gaita-flute performance or documented Venezuelan gaita zuliana context is clear; use Cumbia for the broader Colombian dance rhythm and avoid assigning the label from bagpipe-like timbre alone.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Cumbia
distinguishFrom.difference: Gaita identifies a flute-centered Colombian tradition or documented Venezuelan form; Cumbia is the broader Colombian dance-rhythm family.

label: Latin---Guaguancó
description: An urban Cuban rumba form built from interlocking conga and clave patterns, lead-and-chorus singing, and a responsive dance associated with the rhythmic vacunao gesture.
classificationHint: Use this when percussion-led Cuban rumba, call-and-response vocals, and guaguancó's specific groove dominate rather than the broader song-and-dance structure of son.

label: Latin---Guajira
description: A Cuban rural song tradition associated with décima verse, guitar or tres accompaniment, lyrical melody, and countryside themes, later frequently blended with son as guajira-son.
classificationHint: Use this when pastoral Cuban song, décima-like vocal phrasing, and string-led accompaniment matter more than urban percussion-heavy dance arrangement.

label: Latin---Guaracha
description: A fast Cuban theatrical and dance-song form known for lively rhythm, witty or satirical lyrics, quick vocal delivery, and energetic call-and-response arrangements.
classificationHint: Use this when brisk tempo and comic or topical vocal songcraft distinguish the track from the steadier son and the mostly instrumental emphasis of mambo.

label: Latin---Jibaro
description: Puerto Rican mountain folk music rooted in Hispanic rural traditions, centered on the ten-string cuatro, guitar, güiro, and sung décima poetry, with forms such as seis and aguinaldo.
classificationHint: Use this when Puerto Rican cuatro playing and décima-based rural song are central; Plena is percussion-led urban community song, while generic acoustic Latin folk without this context should remain Folk or Latin.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Plena
distinguishFrom.difference: Jíbaro music centers Puerto Rican cuatro and décima poetry; Plena centers pandereta drums and community narrative song.

label: Latin---Lambada
description: A fast, flowing Brazilian partner-dance style that emerged in Pará from carimbó and Caribbean influences, later popularized through glossy accordion-, guitar-, and synthesizer-led arrangements.
classificationHint: Use this for the brisk swaying partner-dance rhythm and polished late-1980s sound; Carimbó is more percussion-rooted and regional, while zouk/compas-derived material should retain its Caribbean identity.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Carimbó
distinguishFrom.difference: Lambada is faster, smoother, and more commercial; Carimbó retains the regional drum-led Pará sound.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Compas
distinguishFrom.difference: Compas is a Haitian guitar-band tradition; Lambada is a Brazilian partner-dance fusion despite some Caribbean influence.

label: Latin---MPB
description: Música Popular Brasileira is a broad post-bossa-nova Brazilian popular-song field formed in the 1960s, joining sophisticated songwriting with regional traditions, samba, folk, jazz, rock, and politically or poetically focused lyrics.
classificationHint: Use this for Brazilian singer-songwriter or ensemble music identified with the MPB tradition when its hybrid art-pop character is clearer than one specific regional rhythm; do not use it as a synonym for all Brazilian popular music.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Bossanova
distinguishFrom.difference: Bossanova is a specific restrained samba-derived style; MPB is a much broader Brazilian songwriting category.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Samba
distinguishFrom.difference: Samba is a specific rhythmic family; MPB may draw on samba but also folk, rock, jazz, and regional forms.

label: Latin---Mambo
description: A Cuban-derived big-band dance style built on syncopated horn riffs, strong clave and percussion, dramatic breaks, and repeated mambo sections designed for energetic partner dancing.
classificationHint: Use this when brass-driven riffs and forceful sectional accents dominate; Cha-Cha is steadier and lighter, while Son Montuno gives more space to vocal call-and-response.

label: Latin---Mariachi
description: A Mexican ensemble tradition, especially associated with Jalisco, featuring violins, trumpets, vihuela, guitar, and guitarrón and performing sones, rancheras, boleros, waltzes, and other repertory with powerful collective or solo singing.
classificationHint: Use this when the characteristic string-and-trumpet ensemble identifies the performance; Ranchera and Corrido describe song types that may be performed by mariachi but are not synonymous with the ensemble.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Ranchera
distinguishFrom.difference: Mariachi identifies an ensemble and performance tradition; Ranchera is a song type that mariachi can perform.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Corrido
distinguishFrom.difference: Mariachi identifies instrumentation and ensemble practice; Corrido is defined by narrative song structure.

label: Latin---Marimba
description: An instrument-centered regional tradition of Guatemala, southern Mexico, and parts of Central America in which one or more resonated wooden-key marimbas carry melody, harmony, and bass for Indigenous, Ladino, social-dance, or popular repertory.
classificationHint: Use this when a Latin American marimba ensemble and its regional performance style define the recording; do not apply it to any track that merely includes a marimba or xylophone as one color.

label: Latin---Merengue
description: The Dominican Republic's national dance-music family, driven by a rapid duple pulse and tambora-güira percussion; típico uses accordion and improvisation, while orchestral merengue favors arranged horns and larger bands.
classificationHint: Use this when the fast continuous Dominican two-beat groove and tambora-güira pattern dominate; Bachata is guitar-led and slower, and salsa uses clave-based phrasing with a different rhythmic architecture.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Bachata
distinguishFrom.difference: Merengue uses a fast duple tambora-güira drive; Bachata is slower and centered on interlocking guitars.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Salsa
distinguishFrom.difference: Merengue sustains a rapid two-beat Dominican groove; Salsa uses clave-based phrasing, montunos, and different ensemble breaks.

label: Latin---Música Criolla
description: A Peruvian coastal Creole music family shaped by Spanish, African, and local traditions, encompassing vals criollo, marinera, polka, festejo, and related guitar- and percussion-led song and dance forms.
classificationHint: Use this broad label when Peruvian coastal criollo identity is clear but no narrower form is available; Quechua identifies Andean language and cultural repertory rather than the coastal Creole tradition.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Quechua
distinguishFrom.difference: Música Criolla describes Peruvian coastal Creole forms; Quechua is a broader Andean language and cultural umbrella.

label: Latin---Norteño
description: Northern Mexican accordion music shaped by polka, waltz, corrido, and ranchera traditions, typically using button accordion, bajo sexto, electric or acoustic bass, and drums in a compact dance-band arrangement.
classificationHint: Use this for the northern Mexican accordion-and-bajo-sexto sound; Conjunto denotes the related Texas-Mexican tradition, and Tejano generally adds broader American pop, rock, country, or synthesizer production.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Conjunto
distinguishFrom.difference: Norteño is rooted in northern Mexico; Conjunto is the related Texas-Mexican accordion tradition.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Tejano
distinguishFrom.difference: Norteño centers accordion and bajo sexto in a regional Mexican idiom; Tejano more freely incorporates American pop production.

label: Latin---Nueva Cancion
description: A politically engaged Latin American singer-songwriter movement that emerged around the late 1950s and 1960s, combining poetic protest lyrics with regional folk melodies and instruments such as charango, quena, guitar, and panpipes.
classificationHint: Use this when socially conscious songwriting deliberately draws on Latin American folk traditions; Nueva Trova is the specifically Cuban revolutionary branch, while Trova is the older lyric-song lineage.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Nueva Trova
distinguishFrom.difference: Nueva Cancion is a pan-Latin movement; Nueva Trova is its specifically Cuban post-revolutionary counterpart.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Trova
distinguishFrom.difference: Nueva Cancion is a modern socially engaged movement; Trova is the older guitar-led lyric-song tradition.

label: Latin---Nueva Trova
description: A Cuban singer-songwriter movement that developed after the 1959 revolution, extending traditional trova through literary lyrics, political and social themes, acoustic guitar, and selective use of Afro-Cuban, jazz, and contemporary arrangement.
classificationHint: Use this for Cuban post-revolutionary canción associated with the nueva trova movement; Nueva Cancion is the broader pan-Latin protest-song field, and traditional Trova predates both movements.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Nueva Cancion
distinguishFrom.difference: Nueva Trova is specifically Cuban and post-revolutionary; Nueva Cancion spans several Latin American countries.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Trova
distinguishFrom.difference: Nueva Trova extends older Trova with modern political and literary concerns after the Cuban Revolution.

label: Latin---Pachanga
description: An upbeat Cuban dance style popularized around 1960, commonly performed by charanga orchestras with flute and violins, brisk syncopation, playful vocals, and a buoyant stepping rhythm.
classificationHint: Use this when the lively pachanga dance pulse and charanga color are both prominent; Charanga alone identifies the ensemble format, while Cha-Cha is steadier and more deliberately counted.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Charanga
distinguishFrom.difference: Charanga identifies the flute-and-violin ensemble; Pachanga is a particular dance rhythm often played by that ensemble.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Cha-Cha
distinguishFrom.difference: Pachanga is brisker and more buoyant; Cha-Cha has a steadier, explicitly counted dance pulse.

label: Latin---Plena
description: An Afro-Puerto Rican song and dance tradition developed in the early twentieth century, using layered hand-held frame drums called panderetas, güiro, responsorial singing, and verses that narrate community news and daily life.
classificationHint: Use this when Puerto Rican narrative song and the interlocking pandereta rhythm are defining; bomba centers a dancer-drummer exchange and heavier barrel drums, while salsa uses a larger commercial ensemble.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Salsa
distinguishFrom.difference: Plena is a Puerto Rican pandereta-led community-song tradition; Salsa uses a larger clave-based commercial dance ensemble.

label: Latin---Porro
description: A Colombian Caribbean dance rhythm associated with Córdoba and Sucre, traditionally played by village wind bands and later dance orchestras with prominent brass, clarinets, percussion, and a strong duple groove.
classificationHint: Use this when the Colombian coastal rhythm is shaped by brass- or wind-band phrasing; Cumbia tends toward a more lilting drum-and-flute basis, while Vallenato centers accordion and narrative song.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Cumbia
distinguishFrom.difference: Porro foregrounds Colombian wind- or brass-band phrasing; Cumbia is more rooted in drums, shakers, and gaitas.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Vallenato
distinguishFrom.difference: Porro is a brass-oriented coastal dance rhythm; Vallenato centers accordion and narrative vocals.

label: Latin---Quechua
description: A cultural and language-based umbrella for music of Quechua-speaking Andean communities, spanning many local song and dance forms and commonly using voices, quena, panpipes, charango, harp, violin, and regional percussion.
classificationHint: Use this only when Quechua language, community provenance, or documented Andean cultural context is known; it is not a single rhythm, and panpipes or charango alone are insufficient evidence.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Música Criolla
distinguishFrom.difference: Quechua is an Andean cultural-language umbrella; Música Criolla refers chiefly to Peruvian coastal Creole repertory.

label: Latin---Ranchera
description: A Mexican song tradition built around direct, highly expressive singing and themes of love, homeland, rural life, pride, or loss, commonly set in duple or triple meter and accompanied by mariachi or regional ensembles.
classificationHint: Use this when the emotive self-contained Mexican song is primary; Corrido tells an extended narrative, while Mariachi identifies an ensemble that can perform rancheras and many other song types.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Corrido
distinguishFrom.difference: Ranchera is an emotive self-contained song; Corrido unfolds a narrative about events or people.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Mariachi
distinguishFrom.difference: Ranchera is a song form; Mariachi is an ensemble tradition that also performs many non-ranchera forms.

label: Latin---Reggaeton
description: Latin urban style built around dembow rhythm, Spanish-language vocals, and dancehall/hip-hop influence.
classificationHint: Use this when dembow groove and Latin urban production are central.

label: Latin---Rumba
description: A Cuban secular music-and-dance complex centered on congas, clave, hand percussion, call-and-response singing, and communal performance, including guaguancó, yambú, and columbia forms.
classificationHint: Use this for percussion-led Cuban rumba practice rather than ballroom 'rhumba' or the broader Cuban dance-band language of son and mambo.

label: Latin---Salsa
description: Afro-Cuban-derived dance music with clave rhythm, horns, percussion, and call-and-response energy.
classificationHint: Use this when salsa rhythm and arrangement clearly dominate.

label: Latin---Samba
description: Brazilian music style with syncopated percussion, flowing rhythm, and samba dance feel.
classificationHint: Use this when samba rhythm and Brazilian percussion identity are central.

label: Latin---Samba-Canção
description: A slower, lyrical Brazilian samba-song form associated with romantic or melancholic themes, sustained vocal melody, and orchestral or nightclub-style accompaniment rather than carnival percussion intensity.
classificationHint: Use this when the emotional ballad and vocal line dominate while a restrained samba basis remains audible; Bolero may sound similarly romantic but follows a pan-Latin bolero pulse rather than Brazilian samba phrasing.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Samba
distinguishFrom.difference: Samba-Canção is slower and ballad-centered; Samba generally places more weight on rhythmic drive and collective groove.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Bolero
distinguishFrom.difference: Samba-Canção retains Brazilian samba phrasing; Bolero follows a distinct pan-Latin romantic-song pulse.

label: Latin---Son
description: A foundational Cuban song-and-dance genre combining Spanish-derived melody and string instruments with African-derived syncopation, clave, percussion, and lead-and-chorus vocals.
classificationHint: Use this when tres- or guitar-led Cuban song form, clave rhythm, and compact call-and-response establish classic son without the expanded montuno drive of Son Montuno.

label: Latin---Son Montuno
description: An expanded, more rhythmically driving development of Cuban son that foregrounds cyclical piano or tres montunos, repeated coro responses, improvised lead vocals, and denser ensemble interplay.
classificationHint: Use this when a sustained montuno vamp and open call-and-response section dominate more than the compact verse-led structure of traditional Son.

label: Latin---Sonero
description: A son- and salsa-centered vocal performance category highlighting the sonero: a lead singer who improvises verses and rhythmic responses against a repeating chorus and montuno groove.
classificationHint: Use this when agile improvised lead singing over coro call-and-response is the defining feature; it describes vocal practice more than a separate instrumental rhythm.

label: Latin---Tango
description: Argentine/Uruguayan dance music with dramatic phrasing, bandoneon-like timbre, and strong rhythmic tension.
classificationHint: Use this when tango rhythm, melody, and dramatic feel are clear.

label: Latin---Tejano
description: A broad Mexican-American popular-music tradition from Texas that combines Spanish-language song with polka and waltz roots and may incorporate conjunto accordion, orchestral horns, country, rock, pop, and synthesizers.
classificationHint: Use this for a distinctly Texas-Mexican commercial or hybrid band sound; Conjunto is the more specific small accordion-and-bajo-sexto tradition, while Norteño centers northern Mexican style.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Conjunto
distinguishFrom.difference: Tejano is a broad commercial Texas-Mexican field; Conjunto is its more specific small accordion-led tradition.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Norteño
distinguishFrom.difference: Tejano incorporates Texas pop, country, rock, and orchestral influences; Norteño remains more closely tied to northern Mexican style.

label: Latin---Timba
description: Modern Cuban dance music that intensifies son and salsa with dense polyrhythm, funk and jazz harmony, aggressive bass and piano movement, abrupt gear changes, and highly arranged ensemble breaks.
classificationHint: Use this when Cuban dance-band language is unusually complex, hard-driving, and changeable, with funk-influenced bass and layered rhythmic transitions beyond conventional salsa or son montuno.

label: Latin---Trova
description: A lyric singer-songwriter tradition associated especially with Cuba, in which trovadores perform poetic songs with guitar accompaniment, emphasizing melody, text, and intimate interpretation across bolero, canción, and related forms.
classificationHint: Use this for the historical guitar-led trovador tradition; Nueva Trova adds a specifically post-revolutionary Cuban identity, while Nueva Cancion denotes the wider Latin American social-song movement.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Nueva Trova
distinguishFrom.difference: Trova is the historical Cuban lyric-song tradition; Nueva Trova is its post-revolutionary modern development.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Nueva Cancion
distinguishFrom.difference: Trova is an older guitar-led song practice; Nueva Cancion is a later pan-Latin political and folk revival movement.

label: Latin---Vallenato
description: A Colombian Caribbean song tradition centered on accordion, caja drum, and guacharaca, with narrative or romantic vocals and four principal rhythmic airs: paseo, merengue, son, and puya.
classificationHint: Use this when the accordion-caja-guacharaca trio and Colombian storytelling style define the track; Cumbia is more drum-and-flute based, while Norteño uses a northern Mexican accordion-and-bajo-sexto language.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Cumbia
distinguishFrom.difference: Vallenato centers accordion, caja, and guacharaca with narrative song; Cumbia centers a loping drum-and-flute dance pulse.

distinguishFrom.label: Latin---Norteño
distinguishFrom.difference: Vallenato is Colombian and uses caja-guacharaca accompaniment; Norteño is Mexican and uses bajo sexto with accordion.

label: Non-Music---Audiobook
description: A narrated recording of a published or book-length written work, usually presented continuously or in chapters by one or more readers and sometimes supplemented with limited music or sound design.
classificationHint: Use when faithful or adapted book narration is the primary content; use Radioplay for scene-based dramatization and Spoken Word for shorter or performance-led literary material.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Radioplay
distinguishFrom.difference: Audiobook centers narration of a written work; Radioplay builds drama through acted scenes, dialogue, and sound design.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Spoken Word
distinguishFrom.difference: Audiobook is tied to a book-length text and narration; Spoken Word is a broader performance category.

label: Non-Music---Comedy
description: Spoken or staged audio whose primary intent is humor, including stand-up, sketches, comic monologues, routines, satire, and recorded comedic performance.
classificationHint: Use when comedy is the organizing purpose rather than an incidental tone; a humorous interview, song, or drama may need its structural category as well.

label: Non-Music---Dialogue
description: A recording organized around conversation or exchanged lines between two or more speakers, whether documentary, instructional, dramatic, or informal.
classificationHint: Use when reciprocal conversation is the defining format; Interview has an explicit question-and-answer role structure, while Radioplay adds scripted dramatic construction.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Interview
distinguishFrom.difference: Dialogue is any reciprocal conversation; Interview specifically organizes one or more subjects around questions from an interviewer.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Radioplay
distinguishFrom.difference: Dialogue describes conversational form; Radioplay is a scripted audio drama using dialogue, acting, and sound design.

label: Non-Music---Education
description: Instructional spoken or mixed-media audio designed to teach knowledge or skills, including lessons, lectures, language courses, demonstrations, and study recordings for a general or adult audience.
classificationHint: Use when structured learning is the primary purpose; Technical is for tests or operating-reference material, and Children’s Educational is specifically addressed to young listeners.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Technical
distinguishFrom.difference: Education teaches concepts or skills; Technical audio primarily tests equipment, documents operation, or supplies reference signals.

distinguishFrom.label: Children's---Educational
distinguishFrom.difference: Non-Music Education is general instructional audio; Children’s Educational is explicitly designed for young learners.

label: Non-Music---Erotic
description: Spoken, narrative, or sound-based audio created primarily for erotic or sexually arousing content rather than ordinary romance, education, or documentary discussion.
classificationHint: Use only when erotic intent is explicit and central; sexual subject matter in health education, interview, literature, or comedy does not by itself establish this category.

label: Non-Music---Field Recording
description: Audio captured in a real-world location to document an environment, event, community, animal, machine, or acoustic situation, with the recorded actuality rather than studio construction as the main content.
classificationHint: Use when location sound and documentary capture are primary; Special Effects are isolated production assets, while Sound Art deliberately composes or reframes sound as artwork.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Special Effects
distinguishFrom.difference: Field Recording documents real-world sound in context; Special Effects packages isolated or constructed sounds for production use.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Sound Art
distinguishFrom.difference: Field Recording emphasizes documentary capture; Sound Art emphasizes artistic selection, transformation, or spatial presentation.

label: Non-Music---Health-Fitness
description: Guided audio for exercise, movement, physical conditioning, relaxation, or health routines, commonly using timed verbal instruction, cues, counting, and optional background music.
classificationHint: Use when the recording directs physical or wellness practice; Therapy requires an explicitly therapeutic intervention or treatment context, and general health lectures belong under Education.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Therapy
distinguishFrom.difference: Health-Fitness guides exercise or wellness routines; Therapy is designed for a defined therapeutic or treatment purpose.

label: Non-Music---Interview
description: A documentary spoken format in which an interviewer directs questions to one or more subjects to elicit information, testimony, opinion, biography, or reflection.
classificationHint: Use when questioner and subject roles structure the recording; use Dialogue for conversation without that directed format and Speech for an uninterrupted address.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Dialogue
distinguishFrom.difference: Interview has explicit questioner and subject roles; Dialogue is a broader reciprocal conversation format.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Speech
distinguishFrom.difference: Interview is an exchange shaped by questions; Speech is a largely uninterrupted address by one speaker.

label: Non-Music---Monolog
description: An extended spoken performance by a single voice presenting a dramatic character, comic routine, narrative, or interior discourse without sustained exchange with other speakers.
classificationHint: Use when the one-person performative form is central; Speech addresses an audience directly, while Spoken Word is a broader category that may contain poetry or multiple forms.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Speech
distinguishFrom.difference: Monolog is a one-person dramatic or literary performance; Speech is a direct address, talk, or oration.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Spoken Word
distinguishFrom.difference: Monolog is a specific single-speaker form; Spoken Word is the broader expressive voice-performance category.

label: Non-Music---Movie Effects
description: Sound-effects material specifically created, edited, or compiled for cinema and audiovisual post-production, including Foley, ambiences, impacts, vehicles, creatures, and designed cinematic events.
classificationHint: Use when film-production purpose or cinematic sound-design context is explicit; Special Effects is the broader effects-library category and may target radio, theater, games, or general production.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Special Effects
distinguishFrom.difference: Movie Effects are specifically intended for cinema or audiovisual post-production; Special Effects is the broader production-effects category.

label: Non-Music---Poetry
description: A reading or recitation in which written poetry, its language, line, rhythm, imagery, and interpretation are the primary content, whether performed by the author or another reader.
classificationHint: Use for recognizable poems presented as text-centered recitation; Sound Poetry treats vocal sound itself as material, while Spoken Word covers broader literary performance.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Sound Poetry
distinguishFrom.difference: Poetry foregrounds verbal text and literary meaning; Sound Poetry foregrounds phonetic sound, voice texture, and non-semantic experiment.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Spoken Word
distinguishFrom.difference: Poetry is a specific literary form; Spoken Word is a broader performance category that can include stories, essays, and hybrid work.

label: Non-Music---Political
description: Spoken documentary or functional audio whose central purpose is political advocacy, campaigning, ideology, organizing, debate, propaganda, or commentary on government and public power.
classificationHint: Use when political purpose defines the recording; a historical speech or interview may also need Speech or Interview, and political subject matter alone is not enough if another form is primary.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Speech
distinguishFrom.difference: Political describes subject and purpose; Speech describes the formal act of addressing an audience.

label: Non-Music---Promotional
description: Audio produced to advertise, publicize, preview, or support a product, service, event, organization, artist, or campaign, including spots, sales presentations, trailers, and promotional discs.
classificationHint: Use when persuasion or publicity is the recording’s explicit function; Public Broadcast describes transmission context, not commercial or promotional intent.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Public Broadcast
distinguishFrom.difference: Promotional describes advertising or publicity purpose; Public Broadcast describes material made for public radio or television transmission.

label: Non-Music---Public Broadcast
description: Non-musical material produced for public transmission by radio or television, including announcements, news segments, continuity, documentary features, station material, and recorded broadcasts.
classificationHint: Use when broadcast origin or format is central; Radioplay is specifically scripted audio drama, while Promotional requires an advertising or publicity purpose.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Radioplay
distinguishFrom.difference: Public Broadcast is a broad transmission-context category; Radioplay is specifically scripted audio drama.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Promotional
distinguishFrom.difference: Public Broadcast identifies broadcast context; Promotional identifies advertising or publicity intent.

label: Non-Music---Radioplay
description: Scripted audio drama created for radio or audio release, using actors, dialogue, narration, music, and sound effects to construct scenes without a visual component.
classificationHint: Use when dramatic scenes and performed roles define the work; Audiobook centers narration of prose, and Dialogue alone does not imply a scripted drama.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Audiobook
distinguishFrom.difference: Radioplay constructs acted scenes with dialogue and sound design; Audiobook primarily narrates a written work.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Dialogue
distinguishFrom.difference: Radioplay is a complete scripted drama; Dialogue describes conversational form regardless of dramatic context.

label: Non-Music---Religious
description: Non-musical devotional, liturgical, ritual, prayer, testimony, teaching, or ceremonial audio associated with a religious tradition.
classificationHint: Use when religious practice or devotion is central and no narrower form is preferable; Sermon specifically denotes a preached address, while sacred music belongs in a musical genre.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Sermon
distinguishFrom.difference: Religious is a broad devotional and ritual category; Sermon is a specific preached address.

label: Non-Music---Sermon
description: A preached religious address that interprets scripture, doctrine, ethics, or spiritual life for a congregation or audience, usually delivered by a clergy member or religious speaker.
classificationHint: Use when the recording is structurally a sermon or homily; Religious is the broader category, and Speech should be used for non-devotional public address.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Religious
distinguishFrom.difference: Sermon is a specific preached form; Religious covers prayer, ritual, testimony, teaching, and other non-musical devotional audio.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Speech
distinguishFrom.difference: Sermon is a religious preached address; Speech is the general non-religious or content-neutral formal address category.

label: Non-Music---Sound Art
description: Artistic work in which recorded, generated, environmental, spatial, or processed sound is the primary medium, often organized by concept, installation, montage, acoustic space, or attentive listening rather than conventional song form.
classificationHint: Use when sounds are deliberately framed or composed as art; Field Recording emphasizes documentary capture, and Special Effects provide production assets rather than an autonomous artwork.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Field Recording
distinguishFrom.difference: Sound Art foregrounds artistic framing and construction; Field Recording foregrounds documentary capture of an actual environment.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Sound Poetry
distinguishFrom.difference: Sound Art can use any sonic material; Sound Poetry specifically centers voice, phoneme, articulation, and language sound.

label: Non-Music---Sound Poetry
description: Experimental vocal poetry that treats phonemes, syllables, breath, articulation, repetition, and voice timbre as compositional material, sometimes reducing or abandoning ordinary semantic language.
classificationHint: Use when the sound of performed language is more important than conventional textual meaning; Poetry remains text-centered, and Sound Art is not necessarily vocal.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Poetry
distinguishFrom.difference: Sound Poetry foregrounds phonetic and vocal material; Poetry foregrounds words, literary structure, and semantic text.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Sound Art
distinguishFrom.difference: Sound Poetry specifically uses voice and language sound; Sound Art may use any recorded, electronic, or environmental material.

label: Non-Music---Special Effects
description: Isolated, constructed, edited, or compiled sounds intended for use in media, theater, games, radio, performance, or production, including impacts, ambiences, mechanisms, creatures, and synthetic effects.
classificationHint: Use when the recording functions as an effects library or production resource; Movie Effects is cinema-specific, while Field Recording preserves real-world context rather than isolated utility.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Movie Effects
distinguishFrom.difference: Special Effects is the broad production-resource category; Movie Effects is specifically intended for film or audiovisual post-production.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Field Recording
distinguishFrom.difference: Special Effects isolates or constructs sounds for reuse; Field Recording documents sounds in their actual location and context.

label: Non-Music---Speech
description: A largely uninterrupted spoken address, lecture, oration, statement, or talk delivered by one principal speaker to an audience or listener.
classificationHint: Use when formal or direct address is the defining structure; Interview is question-led exchange, Monolog is a performative single-character form, and Spoken Word is broader expressive performance.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Interview
distinguishFrom.difference: Speech is a continuous address; Interview is structured by questions and answers.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Monolog
distinguishFrom.difference: Speech directly addresses an audience; Monolog is a dramatic, comic, or literary one-person performance.

label: Non-Music---Spoken Word
description: A broad category for expressive voice-centered performance outside ordinary conversation, including literary narration, personal storytelling, essays, poetry, performance texts, and hybrid speech with limited musical support.
classificationHint: Use when vocal delivery is the artwork but no narrower Audiobook, Poetry, Monolog, Speech, or Radioplay category fully fits.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Speech
distinguishFrom.difference: Spoken Word foregrounds expressive or literary performance; Speech foregrounds direct informational or formal address.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Poetry
distinguishFrom.difference: Spoken Word is the broad voice-performance category; Poetry specifically presents poetic text.

label: Non-Music---Technical
description: Functional audio for testing, calibrating, demonstrating, documenting, or operating equipment and systems, including reference tones, channel checks, test signals, pronunciation references, and technical instructions.
classificationHint: Use when technical utility rather than general learning or artistic listening is primary; Education teaches broader knowledge or skills, and Special Effects supplies production sounds.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Education
distinguishFrom.difference: Technical audio serves testing, calibration, operation, or reference; Education is structured to teach concepts or skills.

label: Non-Music---Therapy
description: Guided or clinical audio explicitly designed for therapeutic intervention, rehabilitation, behavior change, hypnosis, counseling, or treatment under a stated method or health context.
classificationHint: Use only when therapeutic purpose is explicit; relaxation, meditation, or exercise marketed for general wellness belongs under Health-Fitness unless treatment context is documented.

distinguishFrom.label: Non-Music---Health-Fitness
distinguishFrom.difference: Therapy serves a defined treatment or rehabilitation purpose; Health-Fitness guides general exercise, relaxation, or wellness practice.

label: Pop---Ballad
description: A slower, emotionally focused pop song built around melody, vocals, and expressive lyrics.
classificationHint: Use this for vocal-centered pop tracks with a soft, sentimental, or dramatic feel rather than dance energy.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Vocal
distinguishFrom.difference: Vocal pop is broader; Ballad specifically implies slower emotional delivery.

distinguishFrom.label: Rock---Soft Rock
distinguishFrom.difference: Soft Rock usually has more rock instrumentation; Pop Ballad is more pop-vocal oriented.

label: Pop---Barbershop
description: Close-harmony vocal music, typically a cappella, with four-part chordal singing and bright consonant harmony.
classificationHint: Use this when the arrangement is clearly built around barbershop-style vocal harmony.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Vocal
distinguishFrom.difference: Vocal pop is broader; Barbershop is specifically close-harmony ensemble singing.

label: Pop---Bollywood
description: Indian film-pop music associated with Hindi cinema, often mixing vocals, orchestration, dance rhythm, and regional or global pop influences.
classificationHint: Use this when the track clearly has Indian cinema song characteristics rather than generic pop or Indian classical music.

distinguishFrom.label: Folk, World, & Country---Indian Classical
distinguishFrom.difference: Indian Classical is tradition-based and performance-centered; Bollywood is film-pop and song-oriented.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Ethno-pop
distinguishFrom.difference: Ethno-pop is broader; Bollywood is specifically tied to Indian film music.

label: Pop---Break-In
description: Novelty pop built from inserted samples or snippets, often arranged as comedic interruptions or media-response fragments.
classificationHint: Use this for novelty tracks where sampled interruptions or cut-in responses are the core structure.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Novelty
distinguishFrom.difference: Novelty is broader; Break-In specifically uses inserted clips as a format.

distinguishFrom.label: Electronic---Sound Collage
distinguishFrom.difference: Sound Collage is broader and may be experimental rather than comic or pop-novelty oriented.

label: Pop---Bubblegum
description: Bright, simple, catchy pop with youthful hooks, sweet melodies, and lightweight production.
classificationHint: Use this for very accessible, sugary pop built around simple singalong hooks.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Europop
distinguishFrom.difference: Europop is broader and regionally framed; Bubblegum is defined by light, youthful catchiness.

distinguishFrom.label: Electronic---Dance-pop
distinguishFrom.difference: Dance-pop is more dancefloor-produced; Bubblegum is more simple, sweet pop.

label: Pop---Chanson
description: French-language song tradition emphasizing lyrics, vocal expression, and often theatrical or poetic delivery.
classificationHint: Use this when the track feels like chanson rather than general French pop, with words and vocal interpretation at the center.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Vocal
distinguishFrom.difference: Vocal pop is broader; Chanson has a French lyric-driven song tradition.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Schlager
distinguishFrom.difference: Schlager is more Germanic popular entertainment; Chanson is more French and lyric-focused.

label: Pop---City Pop
description: Polished Japanese pop with smooth funk, jazz, disco, and synth influences, often associated with urban late-1970s/1980s style.
classificationHint: Use this for smooth, sophisticated Japanese pop with city-night, funk/disco, or mellow AOR character.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---J-pop
distinguishFrom.difference: J-pop is broader; City Pop is smoother, more retro, and often funk/jazz/disco influenced.

distinguishFrom.label: Funk / Soul---Boogie
distinguishFrom.difference: Boogie may share groove, but City Pop is Japanese pop-song centered.

label: Pop---Enka
description: Japanese popular song style with dramatic vocals, sentimental themes, and traditional melodic ornamentation.
classificationHint: Use this when the vocal style and emotional delivery clearly match Japanese enka rather than modern J-pop.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---J-pop
distinguishFrom.difference: J-pop is broader and modern; Enka is older, more dramatic, and tradition-influenced.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Kayōkyoku
distinguishFrom.difference: Kayōkyoku is broader Japanese popular song; Enka is more specifically sentimental and ornamented.

label: Pop---Ethno-pop
description: Pop music that incorporates recognizable folk, regional, or traditional musical elements into a mainstream song format.
classificationHint: Use this when the track is clearly pop but its identity depends on ethnic, folk, or regional instrumentation or rhythm.

distinguishFrom.label: Folk, World, & Country---Folk
distinguishFrom.difference: Folk is more tradition-centered; Ethno-pop keeps mainstream pop structure.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Bollywood
distinguishFrom.difference: Bollywood is specifically Indian film-pop; Ethno-pop is broader.

label: Pop---Europop
description: European pop music with polished production, catchy melodies, and accessible mainstream structure.
classificationHint: Use this for melodic European pop that is not specifically dance-pop, Eurodance, or Schlager.

distinguishFrom.label: Electronic---Eurodance
distinguishFrom.difference: Eurodance is more club-beat driven and often faster; Europop is broader song-based pop.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Schlager
distinguishFrom.difference: Schlager is more sentimental and Germanic popular-entertainment oriented.

distinguishFrom.label: Electronic---Dance-pop
distinguishFrom.difference: Dance-pop is defined by dance production; Europop is defined more broadly by European pop style.

label: Pop---Indie Pop
description: Melodic pop with independent or alternative sensibility, often lighter, more intimate, or less polished than mainstream pop.
classificationHint: Use this when the track is pop-like but has indie aesthetics, softer production, or alternative songwriting choices.

distinguishFrom.label: Rock---Indie Rock
distinguishFrom.difference: Indie Rock is more guitar/band driven; Indie Pop is more melody and pop-song focused.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Vocal
distinguishFrom.difference: Vocal pop is broader and more mainstream; Indie Pop usually has a less commercial feel.

label: Pop---J-pop
description: An umbrella category for popular music from Japan, covering varied contemporary songwriting and production rather than one fixed sonic formula.
classificationHint: Use this when Japanese-language or Japanese-market pop identity is central; combine it with Dance-pop, Ballad, City Pop, Anime, or another label that describes the audible style or context.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---City Pop
distinguishFrom.difference: City Pop is a smoother retro Japanese pop subset.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Enka
distinguishFrom.difference: Enka is more traditional and dramatic.

distinguishFrom.label: Electronic---J-Core
distinguishFrom.difference: J-Core is faster hard dance/hardcore with Japanese culture cues, not general pop.

distinguishFrom.label: Rock---J-Rock
distinguishFrom.difference: J-Rock is more rock-band based.

label: Pop---K-pop
description: Korean pop music with polished production, strong hooks, performance focus, and frequent mixing of pop, dance, hip-hop, and R&B elements.
classificationHint: Use this when the track clearly fits Korean idol or mainstream Korean pop aesthetics.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---J-pop
distinguishFrom.difference: J-pop is Japanese pop; K-pop has Korean language, production, and performance conventions.

distinguishFrom.label: Electronic---Dance-pop
distinguishFrom.difference: Dance-pop is broader; K-pop is defined by Korean pop context and often hybrid production.

distinguishFrom.label: Hip Hop---Pop Rap
distinguishFrom.difference: Pop Rap is rap-centered; K-pop may include rap sections but remains pop-performance oriented.

label: Pop---Karaoke
description: Instrumental or backing-track versions arranged for singing along.
classificationHint: Use this when the recording is clearly a karaoke or singalong backing version rather than a normal instrumental release.

distinguishFrom.label: Hip Hop---Instrumental
distinguishFrom.difference: Instrumental hip-hop is a standalone beat; Karaoke is specifically a backing track for singing.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Vocal
distinguishFrom.difference: Vocal pop includes lead vocals; Karaoke usually removes or reduces them.

label: Pop---Kayōkyoku
description: Japanese popular song style predating or overlapping modern J-pop, often with show-business, ballad, or traditional pop elements.
classificationHint: Use this for older-style Japanese popular songs that do not feel like modern J-pop or enka specifically.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---J-pop
distinguishFrom.difference: J-pop is usually more modern and production-polished; Kayōkyoku is older and broader.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Enka
distinguishFrom.difference: Enka is more specifically dramatic and traditional-sounding.

label: Pop---Levenslied
description: Dutch popular song style with sentimental, everyday-life lyrics and direct emotional delivery.
classificationHint: Use this when the track clearly fits Dutch sentimental popular song rather than general Europop or Schlager.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Schlager
distinguishFrom.difference: Schlager is broader Germanic popular entertainment; Levenslied is specifically Dutch and lyric-sentimental.

distinguishFrom.label: Pop---Europop
distinguishFrom.difference: Europop is broader and less specifically sentimental/traditional.

label: Pop---Light Music
